utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone and to you, Mr. Byrnes. We are sorry that there were technical problems which have delayed our start by a quarter of an hour. If I could remind you, Mr. Byrnes, that the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit 0538 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, yesterday when we left off we were discussing an incident that took place in December 1998 in the Podujevo area, and I would like to show you two more documents in connection to that incident and ask you to comment on those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 05348. I see the Exhibit number is written incorrectly on the transcript. I'm requesting 05348. Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you now have that up on the screen before you, Mr. Byrnes?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on the first page, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see that this is another KDOM daily report. It's dated 21st December, 1998 and in the first paragraph I'll just direct your attention to it and ask to you comments on it. It's the paragraph commencing with: "FRY Army VJ forces flouted the cease-fire today..."

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was simply a report that we made to our embassy in Belgrade based on information provided by our team in the field, and the team was positioned close to the air field where the VJ battle group, the VJ MUP battle group was bivouacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And is this the same battle group that we were speaking about yesterday that you had been informed would be conducting training exercises in the area of Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what exactly happened, if you recall, on this date in that area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- let me say, I was not present at the scene. My information is the result of reports provided by our people and KVM people. And what I know is reflected in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence. It's 05348.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01248.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we can look at one last document in relation to this same area. It's 05349. If we could have that up on the screen. If we could zoom in on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, we see that this is another KDOM daily report. It's dated 27 December, 1998. And we see it begins by indicating that both sides continue to violate the fragile cease-fire. And I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 2 which referred to an action carried out by VJ armoured units and Serb police in the village of Obrandza, west of Podujevo. If you could comment on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me begin my comment by repeating what I said earlier, I was not present on the scene. My knowledge is, therefore, based on reports from our people there and those reports are reflected in this summary paragraph. But secondly, let me just say that the -- this paragraph describes two important things. One, is the way Serbian security forces, and by that I mean the police and the army, were working together. It was -- we would -- in our terms it would be a combined arms operation. They worked together in the Podujevo area against the KLA in an effort to secure their strategic line of communication. The VJ would provide covering fire from armour and artillery. I don't recall they had artillery, I think they relied on their tank-based heavy weapons, and the police would serve as infantry and assault positions, in this case, we identified it as a fortified KLA position. The second point I would make is this paragraph underscores what we and KVM sought to do in these sorts of situations and that was to stop it, and as you can see, we did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday when we began speaking about the Podujevo incident and I showed you the first report in relation to this, you said that your units or your observers had observed a convoy leaving Marshal Tito barracks in Pristina and the convoy included Serbian police and Serbian vehicles. Prior to this deployment to the Podujevo area, had you observed such type of joint deployments, convoys which included both VJ and police units?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And before this action which is discussed and described in the document we are looking at today, were you aware of any sort of joint actions carried out by VJ and armoured police units?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not actions that were so integrated as this one was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In what sense was that action integrated? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean by that is the paragraph describes the police and the army clearly working together against a target, a KLA objective, with the army providing covering fire from its armour, and the police engaging in an infantry assault in an effort to take that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence. It's 05349.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01249.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would now like to show you one last document, and it's a document dated January 26, 1999, and this is 05350. This is a report, do you have the document before you, Mr. Byrnes?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the first page, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a KDOM update report dated 26 January, 1999, and we see that the first line indicates: "US KDOM observed the FRY police and military attack on Racak-Pettovo-Malopoljce area throughout the day on January 15th." Do you recall this specific incident?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when it is that you first received information about an attack taking place in the area of Racak?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very clear, I was back at our headquarters in Kosovo Polje. We received a call sometime in the course of this day, I have no recollection of precisely when, but I received a call from army -- US Army major Brad Scott who was the -- in command of the patrol that we had positioned outside Racak. I received a call from him that VJ and the police were launching an attack on that village. That was sometime in the course of that day. My vague recollection it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to a patrol, a patrol and to army major Brad Scott being in the vicinity of Racak. Why was this patrol sent there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the preceding several days there had been an increase in tension in this general area. The KVM which had an outstation in what was called in those days the city of Urosevac now known as Ferizaj -- KVM teams in the area had observed a build-up of Serbian security forces both police and apparently the army and General Drewienkiewicz, the KVM operations chief, called me several days before this and asked if with the resources we had we could augment the KVM patrols in the area so that we would -- we would be -- there would be a more substantial international presence and hope was with that -- with that presence both sides might calm down, might stand down. So we maintained a patrol every single day in the area, and that's why Major Scott was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, you wanted to add something?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to add just for the Court's information a parenthetical comment. US KDOM was made up of US foreign service officers, about 50 per cent of our complement was US foreign service, and the other half were US military officers, mostly US Army, some marine some air force. So it was a mixed diplomatic and US military mission. We were -- we were unarmed. And these sorts of situations when we had conflict my preference and my policy was to put a military officer in charge of the team, but each team always had a diplomat with it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that you had received information that there had been an increase in tension in this area. What exactly was happening in the area prior to the 15th of January when this attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall was that there were -- there was increasing low level conflict in villages around Urosevac and the neighbouring town of Stimlje. Stimlje lay directly on the road connecting Prishtina, Urosevac, and Prizren; and western Kosovo was one of the strategic roads -- one of the most important internal strategic roads for the Yugoslav security forces and it was on that road that the Serbian army, the VJ, had been permitted to establish a small base for one of these battle groups. That battle group was located, if my memory serves me correctly, at Dulje which was probably about 20 kilometres farther west of the Racak area. There had been an increase in tension between the police and several of the Albanian villages in the days leading up to this. The KLA, to be quite frank, had played its own part. The KLA, the Nerodimlje - this was a part of the Nerodimlje zone - its zone commander had become increasingly aggressive, pressuring villages where there were mixed populations, Serbian police had responded. It's a situation in which I would be hard put to point the finger of blame at actually who started it. We got into a, shall we say, an unvirtuous cycle of one little bit of violence provoked another and it just kept building up. And at one point our judgement and KVM's judgement too, I think, was that the increase KLA activity was of greater and greater concern to the Serbian security officials who had a legitimate interest in keeping this strategic road open.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you have -- you indicated that this patrol had been sent to this area to try to decrease the tension that was building up there. Was there anything specific or unusual about the situation there that was reported to you by your patrol?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In many respects this was a watershed. I distinctly recall when Brad called us to report the launching of an attack, he said the Serbian police units that assaulted the village had moved through - and I repeat - moved through, the KDOM position which had been established between the Serbian police units in the background and the village. Let me add here, and I think I spoke to this yesterday, it was our practice and also the practice of KVM in such highly tense situations, we sought to place our people in between the conflicting forces to the extent that we could without putting our own people at serious risk. And our instructions were to keep our people out of harm's way. But as long as conflict hadn't started and if could get in between and at a safe distance we would put our vehicles and our people in between in the hopes that this would calm the situation down and at least prevent the outbreak of fighting. And what was -- what was so important and so significant about this particular incident was that when Brad called we both realised that my deputy Mike Dina [phoen], US Marine Corps colonel, this was the first time since we had been in Kosovo that the Serbian security forces, in this instance the police, had simply ignored our presence, and they had moved through, if you will, they moved through our line and went on into attack the village. And every previous incident, whether it was in western Kosovo, whether it was in the Lap region up on Podujevo which was close to the border with Serbia proper, whether it was in Drenica in the heart of Kosovo, this had not occurred before. So when this happened, I realised, and I'm sure General Drewienkiewicz as well, that something significant had changed. That's why this report was so important. We signalled that to Washington, and I'm sure Walker and KVM signalled it to Brussels and OSCE in Vienna as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see in the second sentence that this report refers to VJ armoured units and mortars firing into the village and tanks of rounds of fire hitting civilian houses. And when we were speak being the Podujevo incident you had indicated that you had referred to that action as an integrated action and indicate that the VJ in joint actions would provide fire and that the police would serve as infantry in assault positions. Would this action in Racak be another example of that type of integrated action that you were speaking about earlier?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably, I would say -- probably the best adjective to use is "coordinated" action. The VJ provided covering fire on target before the assault began. But this -- yes, this is -- the tactics were similar to what we saw in Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this report into evidence. It's 05350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01250.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just before we move away from this document, I just wanted to ask you about the heading. It's called a "KDOM Update" the reports we had seen up until December were called "KDOM Daily Reports." Is there a reason for the change in the designation of these reports, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I can only speculate. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Just going back briefly to the deployment of the VJ company to Podujevo and the MUP units that accompanied that company, after the period that we saw end of December, were these units sent back to barracks, the VJ unit, did it go back to barracks and the police unit, was it sent back to its own garrison after December 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that that battle group remained in place all the way up to the time of the NATO intervention in March. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on your recollection, was that type of deployment, this battle group deployment in that area, allowed under the October Agreements?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What about the police units that accompanied that battle group, did they also remain in the area of Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was that sort of deployment of police units in that area allowed under the October Agreements?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were any sorts of complaints raised with Serbian officials from the VJ or the MUP with regards to this deployment in the Podujevo area and the fact that these units remained in that area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. And, again, that was Ambassador Walker and KVM's responsibility. And I know from my own regular contact with him and with General Drewienkiewicz that they were -- they were -- they raised their objections on this particular incident on a very regular and very vigorous basis. Let me say, I was not -- just to make sure the record is absolutely clear, I was not present when they did so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you refer to this particular incident, are you referring to the Podujevo incident or -- I saw you pointing at the screen, so I wasn't sure if you were referring to the report currently being displayed or the Podujevo incident.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I was referring to the Podujevo incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Until when did you remain in Kosovo, Mr. Byrnes?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the day before the NATO conflict, NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you later return to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I returned with the American military units that went in -- I think, if I recall, two days after General Michael Jackson led the British advance elements of what became KFOR, and I believe that was on the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during the period between your departure in March and June, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was initially based in Skopje, Macedonia, then I was shifted to Tirana, Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During this period, did KDOM continue to produce reports on the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able to obtain information as to what was going on in Kosovo during that period?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily from refugees who were coming, streaming across the border among whom were many people that we had contact with. Albanian journalists from Pristina, some political figures from particularly the Rugova's party, the LDK, that sort of -- people like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the information contained in those reports would have been from people inside of Kosovo who were departing from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you personally have contact with any of these refugees who were leaving Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what sort of information did they give you, if any, as to why they had left and what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- in a word, they left -- they told us, they told me personally on a number of instances, they left under duress or they left out of fear for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was it that they were fearing? What was the reason for the fact that they felt they had to leave?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I would break this down at a minimum into two categories. People who were prominent political figures, for example, people who were in Rugova's inner circle in the LDK, the Democratic League of Kosovo, left because they professed to fear they might be picked up and killed because of their -- the political role they played and because of their agenda. At this point Rugova and the LDK had walked away from their previous ambition or aspiration which was to have the autonomy granted to Kosovo by the 1974 Constitution, to have that -- and which had been removed effectively by Slobodan Milosevic; they wished to have that autonomy restored. They had moved away from that and were now seeking outright independence which was also, of course, the goal of the Kosovo Liberation Army. So these people, when the conflict began and the Serbian police moved in and clamped down on the political elite as well as anybody in the population they considered, I would assume they considered a threat to them, people like Rugova's inner circle became very concerned about their safety and welfare and their lives and began to flee. They initially did not do so. Many, many, many of them stayed. As you know, Rugova stayed and was even entertained in Belgrade by Milosevic on one occasion. But in any case, the people around him did begin to leave. Other people -- and let me address a second category. The second category, I would just call, sort of, citizens generally. Particularly in the urban areas, Pristina, Djakovica, Prizren, Urosevac, they reported - and I repeat - they reported, I was not inside, none of my people were inside, we did not see this with our own eyes, it was reported also by some media. In any case, the other category of people we would interview, we would meet as they crossed border, or we would see in refugee camps reported that the Serbian police had begun systematically moving through Albanian neighbourhoods, particularly in Pristina and Kosovo Polje, and either ejecting people, Albanians, ethnic Albanians, from their homes on the spot or giving them three hours, six hours, I don't remember the details, but it was a very short time. In my judgement, an unreasonable amount of time to leave. And people then reported that the police, when they had a little bit of time to get their items to get some things together, assembling their families, the police would then come to the neighbourhoods, round them up, and they would be herded. And that was the term used on many occasions. They would be herded by the police or paramilitaries from, in this case, Pristina to the railroad station in Kosovo Polje and there they would be crammed into anything, any carriage, boxcar, or passenger carriage, and trains would take them to the border, Macedonian border, at Blace. And we had countless stories from this ordinary individuals, school teachers, shopkeepers, that sort of thing, of this kind of behaviour. These people, I would conclude that these people -- these people were forced to move. They left under duress. Many of them perhaps would have taken the risk and stayed, but they were basically being forced out. I hope that answers your question adequately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Just a few more questions. Were you personally at the border?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this would have been the Macedonian border, if I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was personally at both the border at Blace, which is the closest border to Skopje, and it was the main border crossing. There was another border crossing north of Tetovo in the mountains where people from western Kosovo would come across. I was up there a couple of times. Usually - I'll amplify - I would get calls sometimes from even the secretary of state asking me to go to the border to wait for and assist with, if you will, the formalities. People of some significance and significant political interest to the United States, people -- usually were people close to Rugova who we had worked closely with and had been in touch with us somehow or other by cell phone. They had been in touch with a friend in Washington, they had advised that they were going to leave, they were going to flee. So I would be sent to the border to, if you will, meet and greet. And I did that on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this information that you said this second category of people had provided as to the reasons of their departure, was this information that you received first-hand at the border, accounts that you heard directly from the refugees, or was this information reported to you?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. I -- again, I was at the border. I heard first-hand from people what I related. Other members of my team were doing the same thing, and therefore I had information from them. And of course there were also western journalists, not just American journalists, but there were journalists from the major European papers that were covering this, and we would collect as much information as we could from them as well. And this information was, shall we say, readily available and on a first-hand basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just need some time to prepare for the cross-exam.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Byrnes. I am the Defence counsel for the accused here. And in keeping with the rules of this Tribunal, it is my turn to ask you some questions, primarily those that are of interest to the Defence, but also for the purpose of establishing the facts of the matters you are testifying to. Mr. Byrnes, you told us yesterday that you were retired and that you had worked for the State Department of the United States. Could you briefly describe your diplomatic career. From your CV in the early days you were the first secretary of the US embassy in Moscow and that's how you started. So please, briefly, your diplomatic career.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered the United States Foreign Service in June of 1975. And after our training course I was assigned as a second secretary in our embassy in Moscow. I served there for three years where my functions were primarily administrative. I had responsibility for the arrival and departure of personal effects of our diplomats and as well as the furnishings of our apartments. That's how we started our young diplomats off in those days. And after, I returned to Washington in 1978 and spent two years on the what we call the Soviet desks, the office of Soviet union affairs. And in 1980 I was transferred as a 2nd secretary to our embassy in Belgrade where I served as a political officer for four years. In 1985 I returned to Moscow as 1st secretary, and I stayed there until late 1989. I returned to Washington and spent an academic year at Georgetown University. 1990, I returned to duty at the Department of State and was deputy director of the offices of East European and Yugoslav affairs. In 1992 I was transferred to Ukraine where I was in the team that established our first embassy in that newly independent state. I stayed there until 1994 when I returned to Washington to the State Department. And then in 1995 I was posted to our embassy in Rome as political minister councillor. And as you know, in 1998 I was then assigned to our embassy in Belgrade to head the US KDOM. Subsequently, late -- September 1999, I was sent as chief of our diplomatic mission to the republic of Montenegro. I left that position in 2002 and returned to Washington where I served as special advisor in Balkan affairs until I retired in December of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned an academic year at Georgetown University. What was that about, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife is -- was also a foreign service officer, and the department had a fellowship, it was called the Rusk Fellowship, it was named after the former secretary of state Dean Rusk. And actually the Rusk family had established and funded, and it was to enable a diplomatic couple, a husband and wife team from the foreign service, to spend a year teaching and advising students at Georgetown University. So Jill and I spent that year as members of the faculty of the School of Foreign Service at Georgetown University. We spent most of our time, in effect, mentoring students, most of whom were interested in joining the foreign service. It was, in effect, a year off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind as to tell us about your formal education that preceded your diplomatic career?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated from Yale University with a degree in Russian studies and history, after which I entered the United States Navy and served five years as an officer. And in 1970 when I left the navy, I enrolled as a graduate student in Russian history at Stanford University and from there I entered the foreign service in mid-1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your CV I read that you speak Russian, but I seem to remember in one of your statements I also read you speak Serbo-Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's more correct to say that I spoke pretty good Russian a number of years ago. It's receded. And I did speak some Serbian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say you speak some Serbian, how did you learn it? Is it simply because Russian is a language from the same family of languages and you had the opportunity to practice it in Kosovo and Metohija and in the former Yugoslavia, or did you have some formal studies of the Serbo-Croat language?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the former. It is a member of the Slavic family, and I had the opportunity to learn it, if you will, on the ground in Serbia beginning in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to some of the last questions by my esteemed colleague Ms. Kravetz, you said that you had left Kosovo and Metohija, or rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, when the NATO bombing started approximately, and you said you transferred to Tirana and Skopje. Did you also perhaps stay at Ohrid?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent several weekends at Ohrid. We had transferred a part of our remaining US KDOM team to Ohrid where -- in order to interview refugees who were being transferred, once they came across the border in Macedonia, many of them were transferred to camps that had been established in southern Albania near the city of Korca. So we transferred a part of our team to Ohrid where they could -- once they could cross the border into Albania, Korca was as I recall a half-hour drive or so from the border, and they would spend a day in the camps, interviewing, collecting information about alleged human rights violations and that sort of thing. I visited that team on -- I recall on several occasions either from Skopje or when I was posted to Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you explained, you had contacts also with citizens who had left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, mostly ethnic Albanians, of course. But I'd like to know if you had interviewed or had contacts with members of other ethnicities who had fled Kosovo because it was a multi-ethnic community, or did you only speak to ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall speaking to Serbs from Kosovo at the time or Turks or Roma or Gorani; and I frankly don't recall whether members of our team had those experiences either. My recollection is the people from Kosovo that I spoke with either in Macedonia or Albania were ethnic Albanians from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So only to Albanians is your answer. Thank you. During your tenure between the beginning of NATO bombing and the entry of NATO forces into Kosovo and Metohija, apart from the citizens and people involved in politics, and you mentioned the president of the so-called republic of Kosovo, Ibrahim Rugova and his party. Apart from them, during your tenure in that period, were you in constant touch with members of the Kosovo Liberation Army in Skopje, Ohrid, and Tirana.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time I was in touch with members of the Kosovo Liberation Army. I recall the KLA had representatives in Skopje, and we would meet with them on a regular basis. I don't recall whether it was every day or not, but we would meet with them to try to -- primary purpose was to get information from and their sources on what was going on inside Kosovo. I recall I met on one occasion with a relatively senior KLA officer in Ohrid who had been, he said, wounded in action and evacuated to Macedonia to recover. I talked to him about his experiences when we were in Ohrid. And in Tirana, I was sent to Tirana in large part to have regular contact with the political leadership of the KLA and with the political leadership of the LDK. The LDK leaders around -- and let me start with them, the LDK leaders around Rugova who fled Kosovo eventually settled in Tirana. And the two -- I can't remember all three, but there were three of them that we met with in the embassy there on a regular basis. One was Edita Tahiri who was generally considered the foreign minister of Rugova's government and then another was Naim Irli [phoen], who was head of the youth wing of the LDK, they had succeeded in fleeing Kosovo. And they represented the LDK and they were in effect the formal, our formal, the formal contact between the LDK and Washington. With regard to the KLA, their spokesman Jakup Krasniqi who had been the primary point of contact for us when we were in Kosovo, and by "us," let me be clear, was not just me, he was the KLA point man when any senior western official came in. For example, if Dick Holbrooke came in to talk to KLA people, it was always Krasniqi he met with. If Chris Hill came in, as he did frequently, to negotiate, up to the period before Rambouillet, Chris -- the man Chris met with to negotiate was Krasniqi. If Wolfgang Petric who was the EU special representative for Kosovo, for the Kosovo issue, came it was with Krasniqi he met. So forth and so on. Krasniqi had been transferred by the KLA to Tirana at some point after the conflict began, in effect, I think, to continue these contacts with western representatives. So I was sent to Tirana to be that person. Our embassy was too thinly staffed to do so. And plus as excellent as our officers and our ambassador there were, they lacked the expertise on Kosovo that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In response to another question in direct examination by Ms. Kravetz, you said you had been on the border in the mountains of western Tetovo and that you were there because of reports and information, be it from Washington or Kosovo, that precisely such people, political representatives of Kosovo would be crossing the border, and you said you were there to help those people. But in your answer you said those were people of political interest to the United States. Now, you spoke about the LDK, Rugova's people, about Krasniqi. What did you mean when you said "of political interest"? What at the time was the political interest of the United States?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political interest to the United States throughout the period of time I spent in Kosovo was avoiding conflict and finding a political resolution to this very complicated issue. Let me illustrate my answer and particularly the -- its relationship to my being present at the border crossing above Tetovo by saying I specifically on one occasion I was specifically asked to go to that border crossing, the one above Tetovo, to wait for and help across the border Ms. Edita Tahiri who I mentioned earlier, she was one of Rugova's closest collaborators and was as I said earlier, was considered the foreign -- she was his point man in his relations with the west. She spoke excellent English. If I recall, she spent some time abroad. She was a professor at Pristina University, seemed to be very able. We had been dealing with her since at least 1991, 1992, when the LDK was established. She was of interest to us because, one, she was close to Rugova, she was in effect his foreign policy advisor. And she was one of the people that, looking ahead, we would want to work with once the conflict was over, once, you know, conflicts do end and then the challenge is putting, if you will, Humpty Dumpty back together again so it works. And to do that you need people, you need politicians who enjoy authority at home enjoy credibility and with whom you can work. That was the political interest with the United States and particular in this particular instance. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is an answer. Thank you, Mr. Byrnes. Now, let's go back to the period between your departure when the NATO bombing started, your departure from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and your return to Kosovo. So let's go back to your meetings as you yourself said which were frequent ones between the KLA and the representatives of KDOM and the American Embassy and so on and so forth. Now, my question is linked to that. It's quite clear, in view of the fact that the bombing had started, the bombing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that you no longer had any contacts with the political representatives of the federal Yugoslavia while the bombing was going on because it was a completely different type of politics. The politics of war. Now, you said that you had contacts with the KLA, daily ones in fact, at their representative offices in Skopje. Am I right when I say that those contacts linked to what your response was when you told me about how you gained information that you gained information from KLA representatives about the Serbian forces, where they were, what their movements were, and that at the same time information was exchanged about the objectives and targets, in fact, that NATO would be bombing in Kosovo, that you discussed this with the KLA representatives so as to help perhaps the civilians who were under the supervision, once again, if I can say this, of the KLA. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not right. If I may, let me clarify this point by point. I did not say that I had daily contacts with KLA representatives in Skopje. And the translation on the screen may simply be a mistranslation of what you said. As far as I know, KLA did not have an office in Skopje, they had -- they did have people there. And yes, we met with them. But my recollection, and I think it's pretty correct, is we did not see them every day. Often they would call us. Next point. With regard to military information, and this is what you are driving at, I think. We were of course interested in what was going on in the country, we were in effect at war. But in terms of targeting, we didn't target. That was done by NATO. We had no way of providing targeting information. The other thing we were interested in and we used every source we could get access to, was to obtain information on the humanitarian situation in Kosovo. And yes, the KLA did have such information because they were in the hills where, because of the bombing, because of the military action, and because of the, what I understood to be the action of Serbian security forces, ethnic Albanians and perhaps people from other minorities were being either driven from their villages or they were fleeing from their villages of their own volition to avoid fighting, to avoid being targeted, whatever. They were leaving their villages and fleeing into areas that they thought would be safe, where they would be at less risk. And what I recall was, as you know, you are probably as familiar as I am with the geography and terrain of Kosovo, there is a range of hills running more or less across Kosovo in a north-south direction. They were fleeing into these hills. They were fleeing into areas -- into the hills north of Pristina and Mitrovica, they were fleeing into the hills east of Pristina. And we were concerned about -- we were concerned about their welfare. There were women, children, old people. So, yes, we tried to collect information on that. We sought that from refugees streaming across the border, we sought it from the KLA, we sought it from journalists who had stayed in Kosovo and then came out. Yes. Let's see, to be honest, I'm not sure if I addressed all the points, because I can't see the other question on my screen anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes. My next question is this: Did you, in talking to the representatives of the KLA, give instructions before the beginning of the NATO bombing how they should behave, what policy they should conduct with the local population, and what to do generally? And I'm asking you this because I have information from some internal reports that you were used by KDOM which came into my hands and which I have had an occasion to read, I found that there. But we'll discuss this later.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there still a question on the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give political advice to the KLA how to behave on the ground before the beginning of the NATO bombing? How it should behave and what its conduct should be towards the local population; that's my question.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be a little more specific than that? Are you -- for example, are you asking me did I give instructions to the KLA about how they should behave after the conflict began, are we talking about before the conflict began, are we talking about a period in October 1998, January 1999? I'd like a little more specificity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't be more specific than that. I think my question was clear. Did you give political advice to the KLA before the NATO bombing? The period, of course, is the time when you appeared in Kosova-Metohija, that is to say, from 1998 onwards until the 24th of March, 1999, I believe. Did you give them advice as to how to behave except for a truce or cease-fire, advising a cease-fire or truce?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean to be humourous, but I wish I could have given advice to them on how to behave. This was one of the most frustrating aspects of the job. The KLA was not, frankly, interested in our advice. They were interested in our presence, and they were interested in our engagement. But in terms of direct advice, no. Secondly, if you consider advice, my going to them, either on my own or on instructions, to protest KLA actions particularly relating to the murder of Serbian civilians, the harassment of Serbian civilians, the kidnapping of Serbian civilians and that sort of thing, if you consider that advice, I will have to say in answer to your response, yes, I gave them advice. Unfortunately, in all too many circumstances the advice that I either gave on my own, which I just related, or on instructions from Washington was simply not followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Do you know about the case of the abduction of the vice-president, I think, of the municipality -- well, a Serbian municipality, his name was Bojanic his surname was Bojanic. Do you know about this abduction of the vice-president in Kosovo Polje? And he was vice-president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I remember the case. What I remember, and my memory is fuzzy, but what I remember is he was murdered. Perhaps he was abducted and then murdered, but I remember the poor man was murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. The representatives of the KLA said that they had nothing to do with that. They did not accept blame, but they were advised by somebody to act in that way. Do you have any knowledge about this or none at all?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember, sir, is the KLA representatives denied responsibility for Mr. Bojanic's murder. As to them being advised by somebody to deny that, I have no knowledge of that. We certainly would not have provided such advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Staying with the topic of your departure from Kosovo, in 1998 did you and your team leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We left -- we left just prior to Dick Holbrooke's negotiations with Belgrade that as I recall led to what's called the October Agreement. I remember we were pulled out the morning of that -- of those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the reason for your departure or the fact that you were "pulled out"? The words you used.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that, as I recall, NATO had issued an op order which was the step prior to actually ordering a bombing attack, and Dick Holbrooke was in the final stages of negotiations with Milosevic on this issue, on what led to the agreement. Dick wasn't entirely sure that he would get the agreement. What he was confident of is if we didn't get the agreement, that NATO was not bluffing. They would have attacked. There would have been a bombing attack on some place in Serbia. And he did not -- neither Dick Holbrooke nor Washington wanted American diplomats and servicemen inside Yugoslavia at a time when NATO might be bombing it. So we were pulled out on the morning of his, I guess, the final, may have been the day of dead-line, I don't remember exactly. But we were pulled out just so that we would not be in harm's way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And am I right in saying this was October 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right that the bombing did not take place but that the October Agreement, as it was called, was reached? And am I right in saying that the bombing was suspended?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember the details of the agreement, the most important details of the October Agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that yes, I do, and certainly the extent that we looked at -- we reviewed that agreement together in this courtroom yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did the so-called activation order did not take place? The order for the bombing, the agreement was signed, was concluded; was it carried out?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The simple answer to that question is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May I have a complicated answer, not a simple answer? Why, then, did the bombing not take place if the agreement was not carried out?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the complicated answer is that the sides signed the agreement, Holbrooke signed it, I guess, with Milosevic, and we made a good-faith effort on our part to see that it was implemented. But implementation did not depend certainly entirely, but did not depend on us. At the end of the day, Racak destroyed that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to Racak in due course, although it's not in the indictment in the way it was previously, but linked to this agreement once again we'll have to discuss it point by point, the points that were supposed to have been carried out. And I hope I can get suitable -- adequate answers from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, with the technicalities, we started the day today 15 minutes later, does that mean that I have 15 minutes more before the break? Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I haven't indicated. You could have it, if you would prefer, but we would be equally happy to break now. So it's a matter for your assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd prefer to have the break now, Your Honour, please, since we are going on to a new area, or set of questions which are going to be separate and unique.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have the break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, tell me, please, to the best of your recollections when did you see the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the -- sir, during the negotiations in Belgrade on the 24th and 25th of October. That's my best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, on that occasion, what was your first contact with General Djordjevic like, was he introduced to you, did you get to know each other directly or in some other way, did you happen to meet in some other way?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any direct recollection of introductions. We were both members of a very large group of people brought together to negotiate this agreement. I'm sure there was some sort of formal introduction; but to get to the rest of your question, I never had any direct one-on-one contact with him on that occasion, certainly that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And who led your team, your group? On the 25th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group that dealt with the agreement relating to the Serbian police in Kosovo was led by General Naumann, a German military officer who was the head of the NATO Military Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what did Mr. Djordjevic look like at the time when you saw him for the first time, or rather, what was he wearing? Was he wearing a uniform, was he not in uniform?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory of what General Djordjevic was wearing is fuzzy at best. My recollection is he was in uniform as were his colleagues, General Lukic, General Stevanovic, and Colonel Mijatovic. But again my memory is fuzzy. With regard to the first part of your question, I recall him as very impressive, very imposing, big man, with a very -- a very definite, what we would call command presence. He was a man who was very much in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've just told me that as far as you remember he was wearing a uniform. However, leaving your -- reading your reports and notes from your talks to the investigators, I came to the conclusion that you never actually saw General Djordjevic in a uniform, am I right in saying that? But I'm saying that, and let me give a reference to why I'm saying it, it was from the 30th to the 31st of October, 2001, page 32. The sentence in the paragraph under the title of "Djordjevic" which is D00 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt my learned colleague, but it is my understanding that any references to this interview notes must be done in private session. If my learned colleague is going to be citing from the interview notes, he needs to request to go into private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these the interview notes that you are dealing with, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since he said he saw him in uniform, I would like to go into private session, yes. Yes, my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the interview notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you going to make any reference to the content or are you merely going to say there is a reference at a page?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the part of the statement where the witness -- well, today's witness says that he never saw him in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, carry on, please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As I was saying, it was D004-3079. That's the exhibit number. Of the 30th and 31st of October, 2001, page -- or, rather, the third page, second sentence. And it's under the title of "Djordjevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It says there that you never saw General Djordjevic in a uniform. Now that you look at this, can you state your views? Was he wearing a uniform as you said today, or was he not wearing a uniform as you said then?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said earlier in my previous response was my memory was fuzzy and I don't recall whether he was or was not wearing a uniform. Nearly 11 years later, my memory is even fuzzier. I will stick with what I said during the interview, I think that was much closer to the time of the event and my memory was much -- was clearly more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I just wanted to have the document admitted in that part and then we can go on in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are wanting just that segment that is under the heading "Djordjevic" to be an exhibit, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you really need it as an exhibit? The witness now has made clear that he would prefer to stay with what he said at that time and that what he said at that time, it's clear on the transcript, is that he had never seen the accused in uniform. I think that might be easiest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. Thank you, Your Honour. It needn't be admitted. Can we go back into open session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Open.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, tell me, please, when and how you learned what functions and posts Mr. Djordjevic held within the frameworks of the ministry, foreign ministry, what his rank was, function, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a precise recollection of when I first learned that Mr. Djordjevic was deputy minister of Internal Affairs and was the head of the police -- the public order section of that ministry. This may have been explained to me when I arrived in August and spent a day at the embassy in Belgrade. If not then, I'm sure it was explained to me by General Lukic who at some point after my arrival when I called on him in Pristina made a point of going over the organisation chart of the ministry so that I and my EU KDOM colleague understood the chain of command. But again, to be very precise, my understanding during my time there was that General Djordjevic was the deputy minister of interior in charge of the public order structure of that ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. In this answer you also answered another of my questions that I only intended to ask now, namely, how well you know the structure of the Ministry of Interior, the chain of command, et cetera. You've just answered that. So you are more or less familiar with the organisation of the ministry. Do you know the difference, which is important to this Defence, between deputy minister and assistant minister in terms of functions?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly understand it as those terms are used in our system, and let me explain my understanding, I think that will be of help. In brief, the deputy minister is senior to an assistant minister. That's how it works in our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's the same with our system. When and who told you that Mr. Djordjevic was the deputy interior minister, not assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer. I simply don't remember. But let me add, because General Djordjevic chaired the Serbian side of the police Working Group, my understanding was that he did so because he was the senior professional, non-political official of the Serbian police. And we all understood, there were formal introductions before the negotiations started, and he was introduced in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, I have to tell you one thing, and we also have documents about that in this case. Mr. Djordjevic, the accused in this case, never held the post of deputy minister of the interior. His highest position in his career ever was assistant minister. Generally speaking, so far whenever you spoke of Mr. Djordjevic, you mentioned for the first time yesterday that he was -- or used to be deputy minister of the interior. You did not mention it in your statement to the investigators in 2001 or in your testimony in the Milutinovic case. In your testimony in that case you used the term assistant minister which was correct. Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate the explanation you offered. To the extent that there's some difference in my use of terms, I would attribute to simply confusion and the fact that as time passes, memories become fuzzier, less clear. I think it is important just to reiterate, that my understanding at the time was that General Djordjevic was the senior career official in charge of the police element, oversaw and charged the police element of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That will definitely not be in dispute, but it was in the interest of this Defence to clear this up. Do you know who appointed the general you mentioned a moment ago, General Sreten Lukic, to lead the Ministry of the Interior staff for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know the exact -- the name of the precise official who made that appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know when he was appointed chief of the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have a precise date for that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that you came to Pristina on the 12th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who led the staff in Pristina at the time? Was it Lukic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection, Mr. Djordjevic, was that General Lukic told me at the time that General Stevanovic had been in charge of the police in Kosovo, but that he, General Lukic, was taking over that responsibility. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you allow the possibility that his real name is Stevanovic, not Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, your Serbian is better than mine, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The last name, there's a difference only in one letter. V versus F. Obrad Stevanovic; correct? You said this person, this Obrad Stevanovic was a deputy to General Djordjevic, the accused here. Are you certain of that? Where did you gain that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection was that he -- he being General Stevanovic, told me that, General Lukic told me that, and he was a senior police official who I saw in uniform. Logic suggests that as a senior police official he would be subordinate to the man who was -- the overall commander of the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would it change anything if I said that General Obrad Stevanovic had absolutely the same kind of position -- I have some interference in my headset, I'm sorry. There's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Channel 6 has awful interference, Your Honour. I can't hear a thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would it change anything in your mind if I tell you that General Obrad Stevanovic had the same position, namely, assistant minister of the interior, and we have documents on appointments there so he was absolutely on the same level as General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate the information which clarifies a point that I don't remember being -- having a clear understanding of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us yesterday that General Lukic was answerable to General Djordjevic. Is that your assumption or an inference based on something or are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall is that General Lukic would make a weekly trip to Beograd during which time he told me he reported to both General Stevanovic and General Djordjevic. General Lukic, to the best of my recollection, did not -- was not more specific about that relationship -- those relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that clarifies a lot. Do you remember who was the minister of the interior at the time in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall, Mr. Djordjevic, was there was a man who was not, I believe, a career official of the minister of Internal Affairs but what we would call a political appointee, and it was a man I -- by the name, I think it was Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Vlajko Stojiljkovic. Do you agree it's the right name and surname?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that my -- what I remember is that a man named Stojiljkovic was the minister of Internal Affairs at the time. That's what I remember. And you've provided a first name. I never met the man. I never had anything to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, concerning the relationship between General Lukic and the accused here, for the first time yesterday in your evidence you mentioned that the relationship between Djordjevic and Lukic was such that Lukic was clearly subordinate to General Djordjevic and reported to him. However, I must remind you of a portion of your evidence in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up on the screen P1214. It's the transcript from the Milutinovic case. On page 12145, line 25. And the next page, 12146. But let's first look at line 25. We need to scroll down a little. Next page, please. Lines 1 to 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this. You say that was the first time you met General Lukic, that it was your recollection that he, or somebody else told you that he General Lukic, was replacing General Stevanovic - misspelled Stefanovic here - as the Serbian police chief in Kosovo. Secondly that General Lukic reported to Belgrade to General Stevanovic. At that time you did not mention Djordjevic, nor did you mention the minister of the interior, you mentioned specifically General Stevanovic. Why, for what reason did you mention General Djordjevic in this context yesterday for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that is not an accurate representation of the testimony of the witness in the previous proceedings and later down on the same pages it's an answer that indicates that my learned colleague is not citing this evidence accurately, and I direct your attention to the line 7 through 9 of the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It does appear, Mr. Djordjevic, that the witness first gave evidence about meeting the accused and then he was asked what about Obrad Stevanovic, which is line 19, and the witness then carried on speaking about General Stevanovic, and that led him to speak about General Lukic. So I think the context is a little different from what you were putting a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be that as it may, I would still like to hear the answer of the witness to this question:

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did he have clear knowledge, reliable knowledge, that General Lukic reported it to General Djordjevic, or he just inferred that from the system of police organisation? Because in this writing he clearly mentions General Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, the answer is the latter. To be very direct and very honest, I did not have direct knowledge of the specific relationship. I told you earlier that General Sreten Lukic told me he reported to General Stevanovic and to General Lukic [sic] but my clear impression, and I recall the conversation I had with General Lukic when he said he was replacing General Stevanovic, he did tell me that he would be reporting to General Stevanovic. The other thing I would add was that in terms of chain of command in the Serbian police and Ministry of Internal Affairs, it was clear just from the role General Djordjevic played during the negotiations on 24 and 25 October 1998, that both General Stevanovic and General Lukic were subordinate to him. But I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the screen as I see page 39, line 14, or thereabouts, in your answer, there, Mr. Byrnes, you have a sentence in which you said: "I told you earlier that General Sreten Lukic told me he had reported to General Stevanovic and to General Lukic." I think that is what you said, but it seems not to have been what you intended to say. Did you mean there that he reported to General Stevanovic and to General Lukic or to somebody else? Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I think you repeated the name Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. Nearly 11 years later, my impression remains clear that when Lukic -- when General Lukic went to Belgrade for his weekly visits, he was reporting to General Stevanovic. I know -- my recollection is that on occasion he talked about reporting to seeing General Djordjevic, but to be very clear, my understanding was -- and let's go back to, sort of, chain of command terms. General Stevanovic was the next man up the chain of command. I hope that helps clarify my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Byrnes, have you ever had occasion to find out in your conversations with General Lukic and other policemen you had contact with during your tenure in Kosovo in 1998 speaking of the chain of command, with any documents on their appointments, responsibilities, areas for which they were responsible? Did you see any such documents?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall at this moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. About that meeting that you mentioned very frequently in your statements, the meeting in Belgrade on the 24th of October. On the other side of the table, General Djordjevic had the main role in the negotiations, and you say you had the impression that General Djordjevic had shown a very good knowledge of the facts in Kosovo. What did you mean by that, that General Djordjevic had a very clear picture and very good knowledge about the facts in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that he had a -- he had a clear understanding of the location and deployment operations, that sort of thing, of the Serbian police in the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Reading the transcript, I came away with the impression that the fact the he had shown such clear understanding of the facts in Kosovo was in a way a surprise to you. Is that a false impression on my part? Were you surprised that he had such a clear understanding of the facts? Perhaps I did not understand this very well, maybe you could help me.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't recall being surprised at his command of the facts relating to the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: He led a team that conducted the negotiations on behalf of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Am I right that he was leading the team, he was sitting in the middle of the table; correct?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose that it was quite normal when such serious state level negotiations, high profile negotiations were taking place, the generals should be very well informed, and that includes him, General Naumann, and you; right?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and that's why I was not -- I don't recall being surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, that's why I asked the question, and now everything is perfectly clear. I'm curious about another thing. On that 24th of October, did you recognise in General Djordjevic a professional rather than a politician?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: During those negotiations, were you and your team informed of all the positions and places where the so-called check-points of the Serbian police and army were located at the time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we were, and certainly I had knowledge of those positions effective the day before or so of my arrival in Belgrade. I'd come directly up from Pristina, and we in KDOM had monitored that sort of information as close as we could. We had a pretty, pretty good handle on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday that at the invitation of General Clark and Ambassador Holbrooke you took part in the negotiations as an expert. Can you tell us what kind of expert you were there? What was your specialty at the time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from General Clark and Ambassador Holbrooke's standpoint, I had better knowledge of the geography of Kosovo, the deployment and operations of the Serbian police and the army, and -- than any other member of our delegation. That constituted my expert knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the answer you gave me today, I understood that your delegation was in fact led my General Naumann, but he can see that they asked you to be the person to sign the agreement. How are we to understand that? It's a little unusual, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I addressed this question yesterday, but I'm happy to answer again. Both General Clark and General Naumann decided that it made good sense to have me sign the agreement instead of General Naumann because I was on the ground in Kosovo and General Naumann would return to NATO headquarters in Belgium. And I was, therefore, in a better position to monitor the implementation of this agreement and bring any issues that might arise directly to the attention of the Serbian security authorities, in this case the police in Kosovo. That was the logic behind the decision to have me sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Strong reasons, I agree with you there. But my next question is this: Why weren't you the leader of the team, the leader of the group from the very beginning in view of your capabilities, which you obviously had? Why was it a general going back to Belgium who led the team who would be signing up to this and not you?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I can only speculate about that. I think the question would be best addressed to General Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. During the duration of these talks on the 24th of September in Belgrade, in Milutinovic and yesterday you said that General Djordjevic would interrupt the talks fairly frequently, well, not frequently, but he did interrupt the talks, he would get up, he would leave, and come back. And you make your suppositions about that. But I want to ask you about the facts. Can you remember at what point in time was it that General Djordjevic interrupted his talks with you, apologised, got up, and left? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct recollection of that kind of detail, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't suppose that you could after so many years, more than ten years that you have detailed recollection about that. But do you have any direct recollection of the fact that these interruptions occurred at points in time when an answer was needed to some very sensitive questions? Can you remember that part of things?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logic suggests that the point you are -- you're right, but I would be dishonest if I said I have a precise memory or recollection of it at this point when an issue over -- say, for example, placement of observation points came up that General Djordjevic interrupted. I simply -- my memory doesn't go far that back in that kind of detail. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And were there any consultations on the spot among the members of the Serbian team, or rather, the Yugoslav team, or rather, General Djordjevic? Did he consult the people that surrounded him in the room and on the premises where you were in?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that during the actual negotiations there was no consultation among the Serbian police officers present. They did -- I also remember that they did talk among themselves during breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have Exhibit P1214, the Milutinovic transcript please, and the page is 12158. May we have the exhibit put up on our screens, please. Lines 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, because it has -- it was eight years before today's testimony here, do you remember that General Djordjevic left talks on a number of occasions and you said we understood he was making phone calls. So your answer was that in other words he went to consult someone, whereas today you have -- you take the position that you can't actually say anything about that. Now, where did you get your impression at the time that he went to go and consult someone and make some phone calls, whereas today you have a slightly different explanation, you say that yes he did leave but you can't remember what the reasons could be or why; if you can answer the question. If not, fine.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very clear, my -- in one of my previous answers I said that during the actual negotiations, I saw -- I do not recall the Serbian police team consulting among themselves. And what I meant exactly by that was when we were in the room negotiating, General Naumann leading negotiations on our side and General Djordjevic on the other, while we were present in the room, I had no recollection of consultation taking place among the Serbian police officials on the other side of the table. To be clear, I have no recollection. Doesn't mean it didn't happen, but I can't remember that. Point two: When we did take break, I recall sometimes people get up and stretched and stood around in the room in little groups. Our team did that, and the Serbian police team did that, and there was discussion. It might well have been about where we were going to have dinner that night. I wasn't party to that. But in any case, there was discussion among the Serbian police officials on the other side of the table. There were also breaks when we would -- of longer duration when we would leave the room, and I saw members of the Serbian police team standing together in the hall or in a corner talking. What they were talking about, I don't know. Now, point three: I recall General Djordjevic leaving the room on several occasions.
