My recollection is that he said he was leaving the room to make phone calls or one of his colleagues said he was leaving the room to make phone calls, but that's a recollection of an event that's quite distant now. But what I am completely confident of is that he left the room on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes. Now, the next topic I'd like to address. It's your alleged meeting with General Djordjevic in Pristina, or rather, when you saw him. You said yesterday that you saw General Djordjevic once again after the negotiations in Pristina and that it was a rather large meeting, and the reference there is yesterday's transcript 8186, page 21 -- or 921. You say there when you saw General Djordjevic after the October Agreement that you can't remember exactly -- well, you say it was a large meeting in Pristina, but you don't remember when that was. And then you go on to say on the next page 8187, line 6 to 15, you say: I remember that I was -- on our side -- Nicholas Turnbull from the EU KDOM; General William Walker was there, I think that was the ambassador; his assistant, Michael Phillips, a British deputy; and the deputy leader of the OSCE, General Drewienkiewicz. Those are the people that I remember seeing at the meeting. And on the other side there was Nikola Sainovic, Veljko Dalovic, in fact the head of the Pristina municipality, and General Djordjevic. I quite frankly cannot remember whether General Lukic was there, but logically he would have had to have been. Now, can you remember roughly speaking since not much time elapsed when that could have been, this large meeting in Pristina, as you said?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely when this happened, but given the composition of the participants of the meeting, it would have had to have taken place after the signature or after the conclusion of the October Agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, without doubt, that is the case. I thought you could be more precise. But if not, then I'll skip my next questions. However, since you were in Pristina for a long time already and you spent a long time there, you know the institutions, th buildings, and so on and so forth, could you tell us, this meeting, what premises was it held in? Where was it in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection, sir, was this meeting was held in the Hotel Grand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I see, the Grand Hotel. Can you tell us, since it was obviously a very important meeting in view of the people you mentioned having attended it especially those from the international community, what was the subject of the meeting, what topic was discussed, what was the main subject and the reason for convening the meeting in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact agenda, sir, but given the quality and character of the participants, the meeting had to have dealt with the arrival and establishment and operations of the new OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission which the sides had agreed to. And we had present the leaders of that new mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the time, did you have any personal contacts with General Djordjevic? On that occasion, I mean.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to have to clear up something that you said eight years ago in the Milutinovic case when you testified there. It is P1214 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we have pulled up page 12145, please. Lines 10 to 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the substance of this is the following : In response to a question by my learned colleague Prosecutor Hannis when he asked you whether you could remember on what other occasion you met General Djordjevic, you said: Yes, I met General Djordjevic on another occasion in Pristina. It was a very brief meeting, and to be quite frank, I don't remember what the substance of that meeting was. Now, you mentioned this meeting -- well, you don't mention the meeting, you don't mention any of these important participants or any of this. So can you tell us why you made no mention of these important people at the time and you don't mention that it was a very large and important meeting, that meeting in Pristina? You say none of that here. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the meeting we've just been discussing, and I think I made no mention of the issues that you just raised because of the context of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I have to tell you, working on this case we have read a heap of reports, and Drewienkiewicz reports, [indiscernible] you mentioned Drewienkiewicz, but -- and they recorded or took notes of every meeting and all the events, whether important or less important. And this kind of meeting in Pristina has not been recorded anywhere in the notes that we looked through. So was it an extraordinary event of some kind? But since you don't remember the reason for the meeting or the agenda then perhaps that was the reason?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, as I said before, a very vague recollection of this meeting. I do remember it being in one of the meeting -- large meeting rooms of the Hotel Grand. And given the location of the meeting, my recollection it was a more of a protocolary event in which newly arrived OSCE KVM leadership was meeting senior Serbian officials who had responsibility for Kosovo. It was -- in my recollection it was basically social but, I am sorry, my memory is not clear on that. But I do remember a meeting at the Hotel Grand with this leadership involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. And that rounds up my examination of of this meeting and your talks with General Djordjevic. But did you ever see him at any time afterwards, either in Kosovo or in Belgrade or any time after that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of ever seeing General Djordjevic again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you ever take part in any meeting where the minister of the police, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, was present, whom we have already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of ever meeting General Stojiljkovic, period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next topic I'd look to address is Podujevo. Am I right in saying that the main communication line between Pristina, Podujevo, and Nis in the autumn of 1998 was never cut off, interrupted, nor was traffic and the passage of people hindered in any way on this road? And I'm talking about 1998.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection, sir, is slightly different. What I -- I would agree with your statement that it was never cut off. The Serbian police and army kept that road open. But my recollection also is that there were a couple of incidents which -- in which vehicles -- and my recollection is vague, but I think they were civilian vehicle, vehicles driven by Serbian civilians, they weren't army vehicles or they weren't our vehicles, were shot at from points close to the road. This, of course, triggered a response from the Serbian security authorities and the road was kept open. But my impression -- my recollection is that stretch of road, particularly the stretch closer to Podujevo, was becoming increasingly dangerous for Serbian civilian traffic as the autumn wore on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was just checking the interpretation because there's something that's not quite logical, just like when you said that General Lukic informed General Lukic. That from the positions of the army that were shooting at Serb civilians in cars. Did you mean from KLA positions, the Kosovo Liberation Army, or did you mean that the Yugoslav Army actually shot at Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant by the KLA. Let me add, too, that because of the importance of that road, the Serbian police increased its patrols, its armed patrols on the road to ensure that it stayed open. And in connection with that, that activity was in complete compliance. It was completely consistent with the October Agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was indeed an important communication line, an important route. Do you know -- happen to remember what the main railroad was between Serbia and Kosovo, railway line, or rather, between Serbia and Pristina? What was the main railway communication line?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main railway communication line ran parallel to this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that you are actually wrong, that the main railway communication line from Serbia to Pristina went via Kosovska Mitrovica and then towards Pristina from Kraljevo and that the road from -- the communication from Pristina northwards towards Podujevo and Nis was interrupted and the railway line was not running. So that the main communication line was from Mitrovica to Kosovo Polje and Pristina and then further on towards Djevdjelija and the border with Macedonia, Greece, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, no one likes to admit that they're wrong. You are certainly right that there is and remains a railroad line running from Kosovo Polje to Mitrovica and on north. And that was an important line, and particularly in the 1990s when the Trepca mines were in full swing the railroad was used to bring the gold and -- or whatever they were mining there to the places where it would be processed. My memory is, and I concede, I can be wrong on this, my memory remains that the line running north from Pristina paralleling the road Podujevo, Kosumlje [phoen], and on to Nis was still in good shape, but I concede I may well be wrong. The important point here is that the highway was of enormous strategic significance because that was the route that certainly army reinforcements or army deployments from the main garrison in Nis would have had to come. They could have, of course, gone west to Raska and then come down to Mitrovica, but that was a much longer route and would have taken more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked this question because of the series of other questions that I intend to ask. I didn't want to discredit you in any way, just to jog your memory in view of the fact that the main railway route was this one: Raska -- Kraljevo-Raska, and then further on towards Kosovo Polje and Pristina. But anyway, thank you for your answer. My next question is this: Am I right in saying that after the signing of the October Agreements and after the withdrawal of police and military forces, the KLA took control of the positions that had been left open by them and with their actions in November and December of 1998 it jeopardized traffic, both railway traffic and road traffic, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree, generally, it's right. I would be a little more specific, sir. KLA, to the best of my knowledge, did not occupy -- I remember there were a line of VJ bunkers and trenches that lay west of the Podujevo-Pristina road that were abandoned or vacated by the army. They were in some places as close as 200 metres to the road. We never observed the KLA moving into those positions, and in fact, both US KDOM and OSCE KVM put down strong markers repeatedly with the Lap zone commanders not to do so. The reason we did so was obvious. The KLA in that zone was moving in to VJ and police positions that were adjacent to the road but at a greater distance and on higher ground. And that was a clear violation of the agreement. Now, again, let me repeat the KLA was not party to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's quite clear. Now, speaking of the KLA, am I right in saying that in March 1999, the KLA entered Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just -- they entered in terms of patrols. They didn't enter -- they did not occupy Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of patrols and did not occupy -- I'm sorry, but how could they carry out patrols if Podujevo was not under their control? You have me confused now.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Podujevo was not under their control. KLA -- KLA units operating in the suburbs of Podujevo began to penetrate into the city to carry out subversive actions to -- in particular to threaten Serbian residents, and, as I recall, on at least one occasion, there may have been more, but I have a very distinct recollection of one occasion they kidnapped at least one Serbian policeman. But they did not have the armed strength to take control of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now call up D157. This is a KVM report dated 26 February through 4th March, 1999. Let the document stay on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, General, what was the security situation in November and December 1998 in Podujevo and around Podujevo? And here we see the report that covers that story as well. Are you familiar with the report?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report that covers 26 February, March 4? I don't -- we received the KVM reports because we were part of the international community there. I'm sure I received this and read it. It doesn't immediately look -- let's put it this way: I have not seen this report in quite a while, but I'm sure I saw it back in 1999. Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have questions about that because you surprised me. In preparing for this examination, I found this report and somewhere towards the end I found a portion with a subheading "other locations" and it says: "KLA forces. KLA forces managed to carry out a successful attack on the city itself victorious over the Serbs." So it was not only patrols, they occupied Podujevo after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 2, please. The next page. I cannot see that bit in Serbian or in English. Thank you. The subheading is in fact "Elsewhere." [In English] Top of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we agree that after all, the KLA attacked Serbian forces, won a victory, and occupied the city?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, we can't. I think we are going to quibble over the term, what does "occupy" mean. I never -- I never had the understanding that the KLA at any point prior to the NATO intervention in March 1999 took control of -- took physical control of Podujevo, and that meant they had driven out Serbian security forces. If you want a detailed answer to that, you would have to go to OSCE KVM which had a substation in Podujevo. What I -- I was not in Podujevo when this attack took place. I have a recollection of the Lap zone commander aggressively attacking Serb civilians and Serb security forces in the Podujevo area as we got into 1999, we got closer to the NATO intervention. However, as I said earlier, if KLA had succeeded in taking and occupying and holding Podujevo, I have learned about it for the very first time today. I think what this brief paragraph refers to is that a KLA unit penetrated the city from the suburbs, carried out an attack on, I assume, Serbian security forces, and then presumably killed some people, seized some weapons, it's not specific. But in any case, it could be considered a defeat for the Serbian forces, and withdrew. But again, I was not present, and I repeat, if the KLA had ceased control of Podujevo and held it in the period prior to the NATO intervention, I'm learning about that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, regarding the methods of the KLA, you say you were familiar with these KVM reports on the situation in Kosovo. This was just one detail that I mentioned. However, in the same report towards the end there is a conclusion, and it says that the attachments to the report are the deployment of the VJ in Kosovo, activities of the VJ outside of Kosovo - I did not understand that part of the report - and VJ forces on the outskirts of Kosovo. And there is also an evaluation. It's the seventh out of nine pages in B/C/S, I could not give you the English reference now, but it should be headed "Conclusion."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we display that page, please. Could be page 7 or 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And there's also an assessment. You say you were a recipient of this report. Would you read this first paragraph or let me read it: "Recognising the power of the media, ethnic Albanians will continue to work on international sympathy for their cause. The plight of the internally displaced persons remains their strongest weapon and therefore other incidents involving the movement of large numbers of people can be expected. Careful examination of each scenario needs to take place and one is no longer able to make the assumption that internally displaced persons indicates a Serb attack will take place. It should be remembered that ethnic Albanians monitor Albanian television and such a medium could well be used in conjunction with other methods to increase the propaganda effort. "Over reaction by Serb forces will also be the intention of the KLA - again utilising the power of the media coverage, TV footage of Serb tanks lined up provide a powerful image against the brave KLA fighters in a subsequent shot. The KLA are unlikely to wish to provoke another Racak, therefore the provocations will be in areas they are confident of either defending or at least free of retribution." Can you comment on this passage? You say you received the report at the time and I suppose you are familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's an accurate assessment of KLA strategy at that time, this period post-Racak, late -- I guess late February, early March. I think it's a fair assessment of their strategy and their goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We have reached the hour, we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] May we have Exhibit 65 ter 414 pulled up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, are you familiar with this document that we see on our screens?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll have to remind you then that in the Milutinovic case you were examined in detail by the Defence on what it says in this document here. And the basic point being, or rather, the subject of this document is that it is from the Decani municipality president, he is addressing the government, and it is linked to the security situation in Podujevo municipality. This document is dated the 11th of December, 1998, as you can seen on the Serb original, the upper right-hand corner. And I'm going to ask you about some of the things it says here, since you were already in Kosovo, or rather, your mission and you were already in Kosovo at this point in time, I'm going to ask you whether you know about the events that are referred to here in this document. Now, in this letter, in the second paragraph, the author of the letter, and it is the president of Podujevo municipality says the following: "During the past two months..." so we're talking -- if this is December, then it's October or November that he's referring to, 1998, in Podujevo. "... the security situation in Podujevo municipality has deteriorated dramatically with a tendency towards further deterioration. The final aim of everything that is happening to us today is the total exodus and destruction of the Serbian population from Podujevo municipality and the formation of an ethnic border of the desired greater Albania..." Tell me, please, can these allegations or part of these allegations be considered to be correct? Is what it says here correct or partially correct?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is correct that the security situation in Podujevo municipality had deteriorated dramatically and was continuing to deteriorate. That's certainly correct. With regard to the assertion about the Serbian population, I don't know this but my sense of the KLA leadership in that part of -- in the Lap region, that part of Kosovo, was in fact to drive out the remaining Serbs. With respect to the creation of greater Albania, that's a subjective judgement. I just -- I don't know whether that's accurate -- I don't know whether that is in fact accurate -- an accurate description of the way KLA leadership in that part of the country thought or not. But in terms of the security situation, yes, it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we turn to the second page of this same document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Among other things it says here in line 13 or 14, because it's all one paragraph, that after the Yugoslav army left its positions, that terrorist gangs, and this refers to the KLA, blocked almost half the territory of our municipality starting with the villages of Donja Ljuta and Popovo through Luzane, Sakovica, Burnica, Sibovac, Glavnik, Sekiraca, Gornja and Donja Lapastica, Velika Rijeka, Brodos, Bajicina, Dobratin, and so on and so forth. Do you have any knowledge about that, was this correct? And we're dealing with December and a few months before that.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's consistent with my recollection of what was going on in that area then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now look at page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "In recent weeks this area has witnessed a type of force mobilisation of the population fit for military service into the so-called KLA. Anyone who refuses to respond to the call-up is kidnapped and taken away to their prisons and there tortured and beaten." Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge. I know -- what I recall at the time was there was an effort to recruit however they chose to do so but there was an effort to recruit more soldiers into the ranks of the KLA. The allegation about call-up, kidnapping, and this sort of thing, all I can tell you is that we heard rumours to that effect, but I certainly was never able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you were speaking about the abductions, but tell me, did KDOM intervene whereby the Serbs kidnapped should be liberated if they had the knowledge and information that they had indeed been kidnapped by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little more about that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was this: You mentioned kidnappings. Did KDOM ever or was it ever in a situation to intervene and prevail upon the KLA to free these citizens if there were any Serbian citizens who had been kidnapped? If you know about this at all.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of policy, whenever we learned of kidnappings we sought to ascertain the facts and intervene. We did so on a number of occasions. I remember personally -- it's sometime, I believe it was in late 1998, being in Likovac and Drenica, having been out there to see the Drenica zone commander. I remember as we prepared to leave seeing KLA bringing in five, what I recall were five people who were clearly Serbian peasants. I left that day two or three hours later with five Serbian peasants who had been kidnapped near Vucitrn and we took them home. So we did succeed sometimes. Let me add another point with regard to -- since we are talking about Podujevo, I remember I believe it was in early December a Serbian policeman was kidnapped in front of his house or in the city and General Lukic asked both KDOM and KVM to intercede to see if we could free him and we succeeded in that instance in having the KLA release this fellow to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, do you have any knowledge about the existence of a camp full of civilians organised by the KLA on the territory of Kosova-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge of such things. To be perfectly frank, the only knowledge of any sort of credibility that's come to my attention is that that came out of the trial in this court of Fatmir Limaj who was a senior KLA officer in Drenica. And according to the allegation, and apparently it was confirmed, there was some sort of a camp run by the KLA near Lapusnik west of Pristina. That, sir, is the only camp which I have any knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you'll agree with me that while you did your tour of duty and while the KDOM and KVM mission existed in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, you never personally learned of the existence of any camps for civilians, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, did you in your mission, or rather the KVM and KDOM, were you ever witness to the locality where the KLA conducted executions of civilians, whether they be of Albanian ethnicity who were disloyal or Serbs or other ethnic groups such as some pits or other places of execution? Did you have any information about that, that a large number of civilians who were killed were placed in localities and places like that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a personal witness, but we were aware of reports, some cases they were no more than allegation or rumour, but we were aware of reports of this sort of thing happening. For example, I remember there was a report that I think was investigated by -- not by us or the KVM but another international organisation, it was a report of KLA executions of civilians in a place called Klecka which was west of Pristina. I was never there. I was, on one occasion, and I think it was sometime in September of 1998, I was asked by Mr. Odalovic to accompany, I believe it was Odalovic, to in any case accompany a team of experts, forensic experts, along with my EU KDOM colleague Nick Turnbull to Western Kosovo. We first went to Djakovica and met the mayor and then he joined our party and we were taken to a small reservoir near Glodjane where there are remains of a number of Albanian civilians, I don't remember the exact number, but it was somewhere in the area of ten, I believe, including some Albanian Catholics, their remains had been found along a river-bed or banks of the reservoir that fed it. The allegation was that the KLA -- local KLA had executed these people, apparently for -- on charges they collaborated with Serbia, with Serbian security forces. And we were then take tonne a make-shift morgue which I vaguely recall was, I think, it was in the basement of either a hospital or a hotel. It was a very large building. And we were shown, you know, remains and bits and pieces of clothing and that sort of thing. But that clearly happened. To the best of my knowledge, it was never established precisely who had executed these people, but I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move on to page 4 of the text we have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Further on in this letter it says that: "Already in early October, most Serbian families from the villages of Gornja and Donja Lapastica, especially young people with small children, had left their homes succumbing to the threats and terror and Podujevo municipality offered them temporary accommodation." And so on and so forth. Now, do you know there was this persecution of Serb families in the villages in Podujevo municipality?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about that, the numbers involved and so forth, the way in which they were expelled?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- don't frankly, sir, I don't remember numbers. What is important to me in my memory is that there was in certain locals in Kosovo great pressure from the KLA on Serbs to leave. Harassment, pressure, this would sometimes lead to murder or to kidnappings, in any case, it was great pressure. Podujevo was by no means unique. This was happening elsewhere in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00351.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect that number should be D351 or 0351?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the number should be D00351.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have the next exhibit pulled up, P835 is the number. It's an agreement of the verification mission for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, I assume you are familiar with this document, with the agreement. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with it. Sir, I've seen it years ago, but, yes, I was familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You see where the title says "Agreement" and then you have points 1 to 6, et cetera. I'd like you to focus on item 5 where it says that the: "KDOM will act in place of the OSCE Verification Mission pending its establishment. Once OSCE is operational, KDOM will be absorbed by the Verification Mission." Was that put into practice?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes. What was not implemented? Did KDOM stay on and continue working despite the fact that the OSCE Verification Mission was set up, or rather the KVM?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is that the great majority of US KDOM and EU KDOM resources were transferred to OSCE KVM and that transfer was completed, in my recollection, by early January 1999, at which point KVM was fully operational. To give you an example, I think in early December, US KDOM had something like 300 US officers roughly divided between military officers and foreign service officers, and we had something -- something close to 7-, or 800 local national employees as interpreters, drivers, that sort of thing. Most were ethnic Albanians, but we had a good portion of Serbs. In -- by mid-January, US KDOM had about 15 officers and perhaps 30 local national employees, all of our remaining personnel resources had been transferred to OSCE KVM all but four or five of our vehicles had been transferred to OSCE KVM. Now, the question is why did Nick Turnbull remain as head of a separate EU KDOM outside the OSCE KVM umbrella, and why did I -- the answer to that is that the US and the EU intensified the pace of negotiations with on one hand Belgrade, and on the other hand the Albanian parties in Kosovo in an effort to find a decision. As part of the unfolding of events that began best probably back in March of 1998 in Prekaz, the KLA had grown in size and strength, but probably more importantly, the KLA had received greater and greater support from the ethnic Albanian population. In other words, at the expense of Rugova's LDK. As a consequence, the KLA became to be seen as a political factor that had to be party to any agreement that was -- we were able to reach with Beograd. If it was not party to that agreement, that agreement wouldn't work and we had in front of us the experience of the October Agreement. KLA had not been part of that. Bill Walker and Nick and I and our colleagues had worked very hard to try to get the KLA to accept this agreement and abide by it. And, you know, in retrospect I'd have to say we had enjoyed only limited success. So, to get to the point, both Washington and Brussels decided that they needed to maintain small, in effect, diplomatic missions in Kosovo outside of the OSCE framework to support the negotiations. So Nick Turnbull supported -- it was mostly logistically he supported the efforts of the EU special envoy Wolfgang Petric, he was also the Austrian ambassador to Yugoslavia. And I -- my primary mission then became supporting Chris Hill who was our ambassador [indiscernible] with special envoy. And it was particularly important because both Nick and I and our teams had contact with the KLA in the field and we'd had this contact since the previous summer. The missions, our missions, our diplomatic missions in Macedonia and Beograd did not, so to engage -- to continue -- to try to engage the KLA and bring them into a political process meant you had to have people on the ground. So that's where we were kept up. Now, let me address one other issue. It was decided in Washington and Brussels presumably, I can't speak for Brussels, but it was decided that it would be completely inappropriate for this work, this diplomatic work, it would be completely inappropriate for this diplomatic work to be done through or by OSCE KVM. OSCE KVM was set up by this agreement and had a very different mission. And so for that reason, they decided that was the second reason, they decided to keep us separate. It was purely bilateral diplomatic issue that was not in OSCE KVM's so to speak work requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes, you anticipated four of my next questions so you've saved us a lot of time. My next question, since you are very familiar with this topic and very well versed in it, namely the KLA, I would appreciate your personal evaluation, although it doesn't have to be an expert one. When the KLA actually became a political force.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is -- the question is when did the KLA become a political force?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. When in your assessment did they actually become a political force? At which moment? When did they become aware of that, or maybe they received some sort of instruction, I don't know. When did they become aware that they also needed to act politically, not only militarily.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in I think in a very broad sense, the KLA or OVK became a political force in the public -- the Kosovo public's mind. I think that occurred when two or three KLA soldiers appeared at the funeral of an ethnic Albanian, I believe he was a school teacher who died in, I can't remember the particulars, but he was killed in some sort of incident with the Serbian police. I believe it was November of 1997. His funeral -- I was not present, I've read about this. But his funeral brought out large numbers of people. And at some point during the funeral, two or three people, masked people, showed up in uniform with KLA. That was, as I understand, the first public -- there were rumours that the KLA existed according to the historical literature, but that was, sort of, their first public, if you will, exposure. And that apparently caught much of the public imagination. Young people, particularly students who were active in the student movement at Pristina University began to flock out to the country-side to join this group and to resist what they considered Serbian oppression. And I think from that point on, the importance, the political significance inside Kosovo of the KLA began to grow because, particularly among young people, they saw there was now an organisation that was, if you will, fighting back against the Serb oppressors, if you will. In the meantime, President Rugova the -- and his team were continuing to preach basically passive resistance. And in the minds of the Kosovo population, the situation on the ground and their quality of life was deteriorating. So KLA activity began to increase after that. They became more and more popular. And, you know, certainly, I think by the fall of 1998, shortly after I arrived, there was no doubt in the public's mind that the KLA existed, and it seemed clear to me, my own contacts with the Pristina political elite, the Albanians, the journalists, the professors, the lawyers, the young people, particularly the young people, there was no doubt that the KLA had captured their imagination and they had become very popular. They were increasingly seen as the solution. Now, the other part of your question dealt with, I think, the process of bringing the KLA leadership into the political process. Believe me, that was not easy. Chris Hill expended and Petric expended countless hours and energy trying to persuade the KLA leadership to join the process, to in effect, abide by the principles laid down in this agreement that we have on the screen. And eventually to go to Rambouillet. As you no doubt know, I escorted the OVK delegation to Rambouillet. I went out to Sedlare to pick them up and take them to the airport. Right up until the time we arrived in Sedlare I had -- I wasn't confident that that they would show up and that they would go. It went right down to the last second. I hope that answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Just one clarification. When exactly did the KLA enter the international political arena? When did they become involved with the international community? What is your evaluation? We understand from your answer that Ambassador Petric put a lot of effort into that as did Christopher Hill. But what precise moment do you think it was?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, maybe it's a translation issue, I'm not quite sure what you meant by "when they became involved." I mean, a meeting with a senior official or what do you have in mind? I'm trying to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is when did the KLA get their own political leadership that also became active in relations with the international community, not only internally?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm chuckling because I could read a lecture on this. This is a subject that I've been curious about. I could read a lecture on this that would go on for a couple of hours, and I know we don't want to do that on a Friday afternoon. Very briefly and broadly, I've learned subsequently that the KLA political leadership was actually established in December of 1993. In terms of the -- there were then internal struggles. There was under pressure from the diaspora, particularly in Switzerland, a consensus was achieved sometime in the late summer of 1998 to put together a political leadership which was centred on Hashim Thaqi the current prime minister of the republic of Kosovo -- of Kosovo. And -- I mean, that's the quick and dirty answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from Hashim Thaqi, did you recognise any other KLA political representatives? I wouldn't like to make any suggestions myself. No, it's obviously an interpretation issue. My question is: Can you name any other ethnic Albanians from Kosovo apart from Hashim Thaqi who were political representatives of the KLA? Not only in Kosovo itself but outside of Kosovo in the diaspora.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the former titled political representative of the KLA in Kosovo was actually a former political prisoner named Adem Dimaqi who was not in the field. He had an office in Pristina. He was the formal -- that was his title, political representative of the KLA. The core of the political leadership that we actually dealt with in the field were Jakup Krasniqi, Rame Buja, and Sokol Bashota. Let me say, those -- that was the Troika that we did business with. Whenever a senior western representative came, in particular Chris Hill or Wolfgang Petric, to negotiate or try to negotiate agreements, these were the people they dealt with. These were the people we took visiting American senators. And I remember Senator Warner and Senator Robert Dole who was a failed presidential candidate came out at least once and wanted to meet the KLA leadership. These were the people, Krasniqi, Buja, Bashota, who met and discussed serious issues with such senior people. And just as a footnote, Thaqi was not in Kosovo to the best of my knowledge. I was told by these people that he had left in October of 1998 and was in western Europe. I saw him for the last time, I think, in early October. And I did not ever see him again until he showed up at the Rambouillet conference in Paris in February of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we are going to have to keep a very close eye on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the direct examination the Prosecution used much more time than announced originally. And I am not able to shorten my cross-examination. And despite all my best efforts, I still have two important topics to cover that would take around one hour and a half, that is an entire session, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems incredibly long, Mr. Djordjevic. This session would normally finish in about 5 minutes from now. I do agree the Prosecution took longer than anticipated, but you have since then had very considerable time. Would you like to spend the next quarter of an hour dealing with the essence of the two topics that you have remaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm prepared to make the effort, but I'm not sure I will be successful. But I'm prepared to give it a try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may have to be successful, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That too I will understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have great faith in you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, let's also try with shorter answer, although you are a real university professor, I must confess. Your mission remained together with the KVM, you explained for what reason. You are efforts were geared at establishing political contact with the leadership of the KLA, and on the other hand, the KVM also worked with the Serbian authorities. Just tell me, was there any coordination between KVM and the KDOM in that sense, in their efforts to coordinate certain things?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We coordinated closely with KVM on basically operational questions. For example, the effort to secure the release of eight VJ soldiers who were captured by the KLA north of Mitrovica in January of 1999. We worked together to secure that -- their release. We worked together in Podujevo and during the late December problems there to try to calm that down. On the negotiations, the national efforts, we generally kept them informed or Petric and Hill kept them informed, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D004-3308, please. It's the translation of the Limaj interview. Translation of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this statement of Mr. Limaj, Mr. Byrnes? Does it ring a bell what you are reading on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. From this transcript I will read out short passages that reflect the essence of what he said. He answers this question here in this way: "You know that we established contact with the Americans through Hill or perhaps it was the Holbrooke visit, but still I believe the real contact was through the American KDOM led by Shaun Byrnes who deserves exceptional credit because he saw what it was, he was with us on a day-to-day basis, and he has a clear understanding of the military policy of the KLA. I think he is one of those prominent personalities who gave a real assessment of the KLA. I think the real reason is associated or identified with Shaun Byrnes." Would you give us a brief comment on this statement by Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't see this text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj says that you had a key role in recognising the role and the objectives of the KLA on every possible level including on the international level. Can you comment on what he said, briefly?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw by -- certainly by late 1998 that the KLA enjoyed considerable, considerable support among the Kosovo population. It controlled a fair amount of territory and it had a great deal of influence in short. And what I argued was that we no longer could deal solely with Ibrahim Rugova as the representative of the Albanians in Kosovo as we tried to move forward to reach some sort of a deal that would -- political deal that would resolve the crisis. I argued that the KLA was not only real as a military force, but it had enormous political support and had to be part of any agreement. If it was not part of that agreement, that agreement risked failing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the question whether this Shaun, meaning you, is the person who enabled the KLA to go to Rambouillet, Fatmir Limaj answered: "Yes, I think he deserves special credit because he created us and he represented realistically what we did and how we reacted as the KLA because Shaun Byrnes had spent a lot of time in Kosovo and was always prepared to meet with us, anywhere, any time, and we were open and honest with him." So a very brief question: Are you responsible -- are you the person responsible for the KLA being represented at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, I think Limaj has given me a lot more credit than I deserve. I think that Chris Hill and -- I would add, Wolfgang Petric does not get enough credit for what he did and his contribution in Kosovo. I know that, as an aside, the KLA told me that they would not go to Paris unless I went on the plane with them. This sounds silly, but they seemed actually genuinely concerned that that plane would be shot down by the Serbs if I wasn't on it. So I went. I hope that's a good answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion when they were going to Rambouillet for negotiations, was the KLA promised that if they agreed to the deployment of NATO troops in Kosova and Metohija that they would get a referendum on independence within three years?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was the subsequent inclusion of this referendum on independence the reason why the Rambouillet negotiations were broken off without the prior consent of Mayorski?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked, in response to the interpreter's note, this Paris agreement, when it was amended to include a clause on a future referendum on independence, was it the case that the Russian ambassador Mayorski was not informed of that in advance?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cannot help you on this. I don't know the answer. I accompanied the KLA delegation to Rambouillet, stayed a day or two there to see my wife who came up from Rome, and I went right back to Kosovo. I did not participate in the Rambouillet negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the subject of Racak, do you know how much pressure was exerted on the Finnish pathologist Helena Ranta by Ambassador Walker after she presented her report?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that all those killed, all the men killed in Racak were able-bodied men fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at Racak. I never saw the bodies. I'm not aware of that allegation. My understanding from the reporting I've seen is that there were at least some children. But again, I wasn't there. I did not see this with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that not a single person among those killed in Racak was shot at close range? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that the Ministry of Interior had informed the KVM and the KDOM that they would step up activities in response to escalating terrorist activities in Racak? The Ministry of Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I frankly don't remember that. The minister of interior's address for such a communication would have been KVM, not KDOM, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You are not aware that there exists documentation that the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the MUP staff in Kosovo led by General Lukic had informed the KVM about this?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We have already discussed daily reports covering KVM and KDOM activities. The report on Racak was drafted on the 26th, almost 11 days after the Racak incident, that is 11 days later. My colleague Ms. Kravetz asked you about this. So it was not a daily report. Can you explain how come this report was written so much later? The one dated the 26th.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my recollection is we did submit a report earlier. I think the 26th January date is the date of the Department of State's submission, public submission, of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that General Maisonneuve, when he spoke to Drini on the 17th of January, also discussed the fact that there were wounded soldiers from Racak in the hospital? Are you aware of that statement by General Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are many other details that I could ask about, and the witness has already told us a lot, but I understand it's important to finish his examination today. And that's why I will conclude here. Thank you, Mr. Byrnes, for all the answers you've provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic, for your response. I look at you without encouragement, yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'll try to take five minutes, no more than that, Your Honours. I know we are pressed with time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, just very briefly, I have a couple of questions arising out of cross-examination. First of all, when you were being asked about the period after you had left Kosovo, that is, after March 1999 and the time you spent on the border, you referred to accompanying a US KDOM team that would go to refugee camps and collect information about alleged human rights violations. Was the information that was collected during this interviews as refugee camps later put together in your daily reports that were sent to Washington, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that we pulled it together, but I believe those reports were sent in on a weekly or bi-weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why did you consider it necessary to conduct these interviews at the refugee camps and collect this information?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did so under the instructions from the Department of State.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to a different topic, my learned colleague asked you about the NATO op order and the reason why it was not implemented and asked whether this was the October Agreements had been carried out. And during the course of your answer, this was at page 28, lines 23 to 24, you said, you made the comment that: "At the end of the day, Racak destroyed the agreement." I just wanted you to amplify that statement, whether you could explain what you meant by it?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: In brief, there had been a growing -- an increase of violence in December and the international community also -- and there were an increase of what the international community considered to be violations of the agreement by the Serbian side. And the killings at Racak, the number was taken -- was seen as a spike, a very serious spike. And provoked on the one hand anger at what was seen in Washington, Brussels, and elsewhere as a clear violation of the October Agreement by the Serbian side. And secondly, provoked very deep concern that we were on the verge of the outbreak of a widespread conflict in the province of Kosovo, basically open warfare between both parties. And provoked -- prompted the decision to call the conference, bring the parties together, get the KLA to the table, and try to find a resolution which would avoid conflict and save lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know, Mr. Byrnes, that that concludes the questioning of you. The Chamber is grateful that you have been able to attend and for the assistance that you've been able to give, and we thank you for that. And we thank Ms. Johnson for her assistance. We now adjourn, and we'll resume on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of August, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
